label: Molten metal and moisture
summary: Molten metal that meets water, even a trace, can set off a steam explosion that throws the melt out; steam explosions have killed foundry workers. Water hides in damp scrap, closed cans, undried tools and moulds and wet ground, and metal spilled on bare concrete can make it explode.
signs: Scrap that has been stored outside or uncovered, or shows any film or haze of moisture
Cans, drums and other closed containers mixed into the scrap
Moulds, ingot moulds, skimmers and stirring tools that haven't been dried and preheated
Bare concrete, wet ground or puddles under the furnace and pouring area
A crucible that is cracked, thin in spots, damp, or has been damaged or dropped
Drinks near the melt: water or coffee splashed into molten metal will explode
Painted, oily or coated scrap: the burning coatings give off toxic fumes, so melt where fresh air moves through
do: Store scrap dry and under cover, and look over every piece before it goes in; pick out closed cans, and punch holes in drums so any liquid drains out
Dry and preheat ingots, scrap, moulds and every tool that touches the melt
Load the crucible while it is cold: metal added to a hot crucible with even a haze of moisture on it can blow out the whole melt
Work over a bed of dry sand at least 7.5 cm (3 in) thick, with a clear area around it: spilled metal can travel a long way
Keep a pile of dry sand and a shovel ready for spills and metal fires
Plan and rehearse each pour, and keep everyone but the pouring crew out of the area
Check the crucible before every melt and retire one that is cracked, damp, damaged or has been dropped
dont: Don't put water on molten metal or a metal fire: it can cause a huge explosion
Don't pour onto bare concrete or wet ground, or into a mould you haven't dried
Don't touch spilled metal that has gone solid: it is still hot, so move it with tongs
Don't wear synthetic clothes: they melt and stick to the skin
ppe: Safety glasses under a face shield: a shield alone doesn't stop impact. The UAH foundry rules call for a wire-mesh face shield
Flame-resistant clothing marked EN ISO 11612 code D (molten aluminium) or E (molten iron); without it, cotton or other natural fibres with nothing synthetic, under a leather or fireproof apron
Heat-resistant leather gloves, and leggings or spats over snug leather safety boots so metal can't lodge in the eyelets and tongue
A leather foundry cap or a hat with a brim keeps splashes out of your collar
firstAid: Clothing on fire: stop, cover your face with your hands, drop and roll, or smother the flames with a fire blanket
Cool burns under cool running water for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20; take clothing and jewellery off the burned area, but leave metal or cloth that is stuck to the skin

Cover loosely with cling film (not on the face) or a clean cloth, with no ice, creams or oil. Burns from a metal or steam explosion, burns wider than about 5–8 cm (2–3 in), and burns on the face, hands, feet, joints or groin need medical care
